---
title: "The exponential family"
execute:
  warning: false
  message: false
---

Okay. Why rewrite a familiar distribution in an unfamiliar way? The reason is
that the Bernoulli, Poisson, and Gaussian formulas contain a common piece of
algebra. Once we expose that piece, the same two calculations will recover each
distribution's mean and variance. We will call the shared arrangement the
[**exponential family**](https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=214).

Begin with something concrete. A Bernoulli response can be zero or one, and its
[probability mass function](../random-variables-and-distributions/probability-mass-functions.qmd)
assigns a probability to each of those two values. Suppose that we take the
logarithm of that probability. Recall that a logarithm turns multiplication
into addition, which makes a product likelihood easier to differentiate. A
derivative, in turn, records how a quantity changes after a very small change
in its input. These are the only two calculus moves we need at first.

For continuous members, a [probability density function](../random-variables-and-distributions/probability-density-functions.qmd) supplies density rather than point mass. The derivatives below recover [expectation and variance](../random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance.qmd). When we hold the observed responses fixed and vary the parameter, the same expression becomes a [likelihood](../statistical-inference/maximum-likelihood.qmd).

We first rewrite a Bernoulli mass, then generalize its algebra, recover the mean
and variance, and map the Poisson and Gaussian families into the same template.

## Beginning with Bernoulli choices

In the SuperTelicity data, let \(Y_i=1\) mark an *in* response and \(Y_i=0\)
mark a *for* response. The observed counts anchor the distribution we will
rewrite:

```{r}
#| label: observed-bernoulli-mass
#| echo: true
st <- read.csv("data/supertelicity/supertelicity-cloze.csv")
counts <- as.data.frame(table(st$preposition))
names(counts) <- c("preposition", "observations")
counts$probability <- counts$observations / sum(counts$observations)
counts
```

The Bernoulli mean--variance relation is visible across observed subsets of the
same experiment. The temporal magnitude used to form those subsets was elicited
together with the participant's *in* or *for* choice. It was not a duration
measured before that choice. Moreover, a magnitude is retained only for
episodic trials, which describe a particular event; generic trials describe an
event kind and have no value on this measure. The grouped
relation below is therefore a descriptive association between two jointly
elicited parts of the episodic response.

The code divides the selected temporal magnitude into observed quantile groups
within each verb type, computes the *in* proportion in each group, and then
obtains the Bernoulli variance $\widehat\pi(1-\widehat\pi)$ from that observed
proportion.

```{r}
#| label: plot-observed-bernoulli-mean-variance
#| echo: true
library(ggplot2)
st_duration <- st[
  st$clause_type == "episodic" & !is.na(st$log_duration_minutes),
]
stopifnot(nrow(st_duration) > 0L, all(st_duration$clause_type == "episodic"))
duration_breaks <- unique(quantile(
  st_duration$log_duration_minutes,
  probs = seq(0, 1, length.out = 7L)
))
st_duration$duration_group <- cut(
  st_duration$log_duration_minutes,
  breaks = duration_breaks,
  include.lowest = TRUE
)
observed_mean_variance <- aggregate(
  prep_in ~ verb_type + duration_group,
  st_duration,
  function(values) c(probability = mean(values), observations = length(values))
)
observed_mean_variance <- data.frame(
  verb_type = observed_mean_variance$verb_type,
  duration_group = observed_mean_variance$duration_group,
  probability = observed_mean_variance$prep_in[, "probability"],
  observations = observed_mean_variance$prep_in[, "observations"]
)
observed_mean_variance$bernoulli_variance <- with(
  observed_mean_variance,
  probability * (1 - probability)
)
ggplot(observed_mean_variance,
       aes(probability, bernoulli_variance, shape = verb_type,
           size = observations)) +
  geom_point(color = "#1F5A85") +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 4) +
  labs(x = "Observed probability of an in-completion",
       y = "Bernoulli variance",
       shape = NULL, size = "Observed rows") +
  theme_classic()
```

Every vertical coordinate is calculated directly from its observed group probability, so the connecting arch serves only as a visual guide. The plot shows the algebraic fact we will recover below: Bernoulli variance is small near probability zero or one and largest near one half.

For one fixed response \(y_i\in\{0,1\}\), the Bernoulli mass is

$$
p(y_i\mid\pi_i)=\pi_i^{y_i}(1-\pi_i)^{1-y_i}.
$$

Define the log-odds parameter
\(\theta_i=\log[\pi_i/(1-\pi_i)]\), so
\(\pi_i=e^{\theta_i}/(1+e^{\theta_i})\). Taking logs and substituting gives

$$
\log p(y_i\mid\theta_i)
=y_i\theta_i-\log(1+e^{\theta_i}).
$$

Two pieces are now visible: the observed value \(y_i\) multiplies
\(\theta_i\), while \(\log(1+e^{\theta_i})\) makes the two Bernoulli masses sum
to one. The exponential-family form names and generalizes those pieces.

## Generalizing the pattern

The form below is the **one-parameter exponential dispersion family**: one
canonical parameter $\theta$ controls the conditional mean, while $\phi$
controls dispersion. More general exponential families can have vectors of
canonical parameters.

$$
p(y\mid\theta,\phi)=\exp\left\{\frac{y\theta-b(\theta)}{a(\phi)}+c(y,\phi)\right\}.
$$

For an absolutely continuous member, the same form is written as a PDF
\(f(y\mid\theta,\phi)\). We use \(p\) for the discrete Bernoulli member above.

The **canonical parameter** \(\theta\) is the parameter that multiplies the
response \(y\) directly in the exponent. The function \(b(\theta)\) will
determine the mean and variance. The parameter \(\phi\) controls the variation
left after the mean has been fixed; we call it the **dispersion parameter**, and
\(a(\phi)\) places that dispersion on the scale used in the exponent. Finally,
\(c(y,\phi)\) contains the response and dispersion terms needed to make the
total mass or density equal one.

The notation \(d\nu(y)\) below lets one equation cover two cases. For a
discrete response, the integral means that we sum over every possible value of
\(y\). For a continuous response, it means that we integrate over those values.
We can now start from the requirement that the total probability equals one:

$$
1=\int \exp\left\{\frac{y\theta-b(\theta)}{a(\phi)}+c(y,\phi)\right\}\,d\nu(y).
$$

The next step uses a derivative, which measures [local change as its input
moves](../random-variables-and-distributions/expected-values.qmd#derivatives-as-local-rates-of-change).
Under the tail condition stated in the technical note below, we may
differentiate both sides with respect to \(\theta\) and move the derivative
inside the integral. The left side is zero because the derivative of the
constant one is zero, so

$$
0=\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{Y-b'(\theta)}{a(\phi)}\right],
\qquad\text{and thus}\qquad
\mathbb{E}[Y]=b'(\theta).
$$

To obtain the variance, differentiate the first identity once more. The
derivative of the density contributes its score
$(Y-b'(\theta))/a(\phi)$, while differentiating $-b'(\theta)$ contributes
$-b''(\theta)$. Thus

$$
0
=
-\frac{b''(\theta)}{a(\phi)}
+
\mathbb{E}\left[
\frac{(Y-b'(\theta))^2}{a(\phi)^2}
\right].
$$

We already know that $b'(\theta)=\mathbb{E}[Y]$, so the expectation in the
second term is $\operatorname{Var}[Y]/a(\phi)^2$. Multiplying through by
$a(\phi)^2$ gives

$$
\operatorname{Var}[Y]=a(\phi)b''(\theta).
$$

These same derivatives guide likelihood optimization. For one observed value
\(y\), the log likelihood is

$$
\ell(\theta;y)
=
\frac{y\theta-b(\theta)}{a(\phi)}
+c(y,\phi).
$$

Its **score** is the derivative with respect to the parameter:

$$
\frac{\partial\ell(\theta;y)}{\partial\theta}
=
\frac{y-b'(\theta)}{a(\phi)}.
$$

A positive score says that a small increase in \(\theta\) would raise the log
likelihood locally; a negative score points toward a decrease. The second
derivative is

$$
\frac{\partial^2\ell(\theta;y)}{\partial\theta^2}
=
-\frac{b''(\theta)}{a(\phi)}.
$$

With several parameters, the **Hessian** collects all such second derivatives
and cross-derivatives in a matrix; the [Hessian
discussion](../statistical-inference/beyond-conjugacy.qmd#hessian-as-local-curvature)
develops that local-curvature interpretation. For independent observations,
the log likelihood, score, and Hessian each add their observation-level
contributions.

For the Bernoulli calculation above,
\(b(\theta)=\log(1+e^\theta)\) and \(a(\phi)=1\). Its first two derivatives
recover \(b'(\theta)=\pi\) and \(b''(\theta)=\pi(1-\pi)\).

<details>
<summary>When may we differentiate inside the integral?</summary>

Moving a derivative inside an integral requires a **regularity condition**.
For \(\theta\) in a neighborhood of the value under study, suppose the absolute
derivative of the integrand stays below one common function whose integral is
finite. This condition is called **domination**. It rules out a situation in
which a small parameter change sends substantial derivative mass into the
tails, and it justifies exchanging the derivative and integral above. The
second-derivative identity requires the corresponding condition for the next
derivative.

</details>

## Mapping the Poisson PMF into the template

Start with

$$
p(y\mid\lambda)
=e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^y}{y!}.
$$

Setting $\theta=\log\lambda$ gives $\lambda=e^\theta$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}
\log p(y\mid\theta)
&=-e^\theta+y\theta-\log(y!)\\
&=\frac{y\theta-b(\theta)}{a(\phi)}+c(y,\phi),
\end{aligned}
$$

with $b(\theta)=e^\theta$, $a(\phi)=1$, and $c(y,\phi)=-\log(y!)$. The derivatives are $b'(\theta)=e^\theta=\lambda$ and $b''(\theta)=e^\theta=\lambda$, which recover the Poisson mean and variance. This substitution is the operation summarized by the Poisson row of the table; the table is a cross-check rather than a new list of formulas to memorize. <!-- dqr-allow: symbolic-derivation -->

| Family | $\theta$ | $b(\theta)$ | $a(\phi)$ | Mean | Variance |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Bernoulli | $\log[\pi/(1-\pi)]$ | $\log(1+e^\theta)$ | $1$ | $\pi$ | $\pi(1-\pi)$ |
| Poisson | $\log\lambda$ | $e^\theta$ | $1$ | $\lambda$ | $\lambda$ |
| Normal with known variance $\sigma^2$ | $\mu$ | $\theta^2/2$ | $\sigma^2$ | $\mu$ | $\sigma^2$ |

```{r}
#| label: observed-bernoulli-likelihood
#| echo: true
y <- st$prep_in
pi_hat <- mean(y)
log_likelihood <- sum(dbinom(y, size = 1L, prob = pi_hat, log = TRUE))
c(rows = length(y), in_responses = sum(y), probability_in = pi_hat,
  log_likelihood = log_likelihood,
  bernoulli_variance = pi_hat * (1 - pi_hat))
```

The shared form links distributions to GLM computation, but it does not make the families interchangeable. Bernoulli, Poisson, and normal models retain different supports and mean–variance relations. The exponential-family notation organizes those distinctions; it does not remove them.

## Recap and check

1. Does membership in the exponential family allow a Poisson model for binary data? No. Family membership does not erase support or variance restrictions.
2. What work does $c(y,\phi)$ do? It contains response-dependent terms, including the base measure, required for normalization even when those terms do not contain $\theta$.

We can use the same factorized likelihood to ask which sample features retain information about a parameter. This leads to [sufficient statistics](sufficient-statistics.qmd).
